newsitem.title: USA: U.S. requires warning on "Herbal Ecstacy".
newsitem.headline: U.S. requires warning on "Herbal Ecstacy".

text.p: The supplement Herbal Ecstacy has health and safety risks which must be highlighted in future advertising by its marketer, the government announced Tuesday.
The Federal Trade Commission said Global World Media Inc. has agreed to issue a warning label, in an order which will take effect in 60 days.

The FTC said Global World has also agreed to stop claiming the product is entirely safe and will put the following warning label on the supplement: "Warning: This product contains ephedrine which can have dangerous effects on the central nervous system and heart and could result in serious injury. Risk of injury increases with dose."
Global World and its owner, Sean Shayan, also agreed not to promote the supplement as a euphoric, for sexual effects or as an alternative to an illegal drug.
Herbal Ecstacy's main ingredient is the herb ephedra, known also as Ma-Huang, which is a natural source of ephedrine alkaloids, the FTC said.

Jodie Bernstein, director of the FTC's Bureau of Consumer Protection, said the death of at least one college student in Florida "was directly attributed to taking a large dose of a product similar to Ecstacy."

When Reuters called the company for comment, the person who answered identified himself as Victor Mackey, the "graveyard shift telemarketer." Mackey said he was there to respond to magazine ads and said of the product:
"It's basically a really fun experience...you feel really good," he said. "Like, have you ever gone out and felt really good and motivated to do something that you normally don't do?
"It's safe and completely there's no side effects," he said. "There's nothing bad about this product at all."
Mackey said the label advised taking only one tablet every 72 hours, but that he has taken three to five at a time himself. He said the company sells 10 tablets for $19.95.

At one time the company's ads advised consumers to take as many as five tablet at a time. That dose is nearly eight times the amount of ephedra which the FDA says in a proposed rule should be the serving size.
The FTC also said Global World's ads relied on an endorsement from a "Dr. Steven Jonson of Tel Aviv who, in fact, is a fictitious person."
The company's lawyer, William Dailey of Encinco, Calif., was not immediately available for comment.
The FTC has no authority to fine companies in agreements like those made with Global World unless companies violate the order.
